stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
When the province of Easton raised its minimum wage by 9 percent in 2019, economist Rana Celik tracked staffing at 400 restaurants. A year later, headcounts were statistically unchanged from those in a neighboring province that had no increase. Celik thus concluded that the raise left low-wage workers no worse off.

Text 2
Celik is right that Easton's restaurants did not shed workers after the raise. But headcount is a blunt measure. Payroll records from the same period show that average weekly hours per employee fell by nearly three, so many workers may have taken home less despite keeping their jobs.
choices: The 2019 raise left Easton's low-wage restaurant workers no worse off overall.
Restaurant employment in Easton held roughly steady in the year after the raise.
Easton's restaurants absorbed the higher wage mainly by cutting weekly hours.
Comparing Easton with a neighboring province is the best way to judge the raise.
explanation: The authors disagree about whether workers were harmed, but both accept the headcount finding. Text 1 reports that headcounts were 'statistically unchanged,' and Text 2 concedes that the restaurants 'did not shed workers.' Each text has a sentence that supports this choice.

A.why: You picked Text 1's side of the disagreement. This is Celik's conclusion, and Text 2 exists to challenge it by arguing that reduced hours may have cut workers' pay.

C.why: You picked Text 2's side, and in a stronger form than Text 2 states it. Text 1 never mentions hours, and Text 2 says only that hours fell. It does not say that cutting hours was the restaurants' main response.

D.why: Text 1 uses a neighboring province for comparison but never calls it the best method, and Text 2 says nothing about it. Neither text supports this claim.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Versions of the bridge-bargain tale, in which a builder promises a river spirit the first living thing to cross, appear in over thirty villages along the Varn River. Nearly all end with the builder sending a goat across first. Folklorist Ilse Maran therefore argues that the tale spread from one source along river trade routes.

Text 2
The resemblance among the Varn versions is real, but a shared ending need not mean a shared origin. Goats were the cheapest livestock in the region, so storytellers could have independently chosen one as the obvious thing to sacrifice.
choices: The tale reached the Varn villages by traveling along river trade routes.
Storytellers picked the goat because it was the region's least valuable animal.
The Varn River versions of the tale share a strikingly similar ending.
The tale is older than any other story recorded along the Varn River.
explanation: The authors disagree about why the versions match: one source, or separate invention. Both accept that they do match. Text 1 says 'nearly all end with the builder sending a goat across first,' and Text 2 grants that 'the resemblance among the Varn versions is real.'

A.why: You picked Text 1's side of the disagreement. Text 2 directly disputes this by saying that 'a shared ending need not mean a shared origin.'

B.why: You picked Text 2's explanation, and Text 2 only says storytellers 'could have' chosen the goat for this reason. Text 1 never discusses why the goat was chosen.

D.why: Neither text compares the tale's age with other local stories. You inferred something that neither passage supports.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Surveying 120 reefs across the western Pacific during the 2024 marine heat wave, biologist Tomás Reyes found that bleaching rose sharply wherever water stayed more than 1°C above the seasonal maximum for four weeks. He concluded that every reef crossing that threshold should be expected to bleach.

Text 2
Heat stress certainly drives bleaching, but not uniformly. In muddy coastal bays off Sulawesi, reefs that crossed Reyes's threshold bleached far less than clear-water reefs did, likely because suspended sediment shaded corals from the intense sunlight that compounds heat damage.
choices: Prolonged high water temperatures are a major cause of coral bleaching.
Any reef that stays above the threshold for four weeks will bleach.
Muddy water shields corals from sunlight that worsens heat damage.
Sulawesi's reefs recovered from the 2024 heat wave faster than others.
explanation: The disagreement is about whether the threshold predicts bleaching on every reef. Underneath it, both authors treat heat as a driver. Text 1 links bleaching to water that stayed above the seasonal maximum, and Text 2 opens by granting that 'heat stress certainly drives bleaching.'

B.why: This is Text 1's broad conclusion, and it is exactly what Text 2 narrows. The Sulawesi reefs crossed the threshold and bleached far less.

C.why: Only Text 2 offers this explanation, and it hedges with 'likely.' Text 1 says nothing about sediment or sunlight, so this choice fails the check against Text 1.

D.why: Neither text discusses recovery. Text 2 compares how much the reefs bleached, not how fast they recovered.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Linguist Amara Osei compared recordings of Brennick residents born between 1900 and 1990 and found that speakers born after 1950 pronounce “pool” and “pull” identically, while older speakers keep them distinct. Osei therefore dates the onset of the merger to the mid-twentieth century.

Text 2
Osei's recordings clearly document the merger in Brennick speech. Yet recordings capture only careful speech. Diaries kept by Brennick schoolchildren in the 1920s already rhyme “pool” with “full,” suggesting the merger was under way in casual use decades earlier than Osei proposes.
choices: The merger began among Brennick speakers born around the year 1950.
The merger first appeared in Brennick speech in the 1920s or earlier.
Children's diaries record speech more reliably than audio recordings do.
The vowels in “pool” and “pull” have merged in much of Brennick speech.
explanation: The authors disagree about when the merger began. Both accept that it happened. Text 1 reports that younger speakers pronounce the two words 'identically,' and Text 2 says that Osei's recordings 'clearly document the merger in Brennick speech.'

A.why: You picked Text 1's side of the dating dispute. Text 2 argues that the merger was under way decades before 1950.

B.why: You picked Text 2's side of the dating dispute. Text 1 places the onset in the mid-twentieth century, so Osei would reject this.

C.why: Text 2 says only that recordings capture careful speech. It never claims that diaries are more reliable overall, and Text 1 does not mention diaries.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Road salt seeps into concrete bridge decks and corrodes the steel reinforcement inside. Inspecting 60 decks in a northern state, engineer Dana Whitlock found that those treated with a silane sealer showed half as much corrosion after fifteen years as untreated decks. She therefore recommends sealing every deck in states that salt their roads.

Text 2
Keeping salt out of concrete is indeed the key to a long-lived deck. But sealers wear away under traffic and must be reapplied every few years. For new decks, a dense, low-permeability concrete mix blocks salt for decades without that upkeep.
choices: Every bridge deck in states that salt roads should be treated with a sealer.
Limiting how much salt enters a deck's concrete helps the deck last longer.
Low-permeability concrete is a better choice than sealer for new decks.
Sealers protect bridge decks more effectively in some climates than others.
explanation: The authors disagree about how to keep salt out, sealer or denser concrete. Both agree that keeping it out is the goal. Text 1 says that salt corrodes the reinforcement and that sealed decks corroded less, and Text 2 grants that 'keeping salt out of concrete is indeed the key to a long-lived deck.'

A.why: This is Whitlock's recommendation. Text 2 argues against it, at least for new decks, so it is one side of the disagreement.

C.why: This is Text 2's position, but Text 1 never mentions concrete mixes. A statement that only one author supports does not pass the check against both texts.

D.why: Neither text compares climates. Text 1 studies decks in one state only, and Text 2 does not address location.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Older adults often lose muscle partly because they eat too little protein. In a twelve-week trial, nutrition scientist Priya Raman found that adults over 65 who split their protein evenly across three meals gained more leg strength than those who ate most of it at dinner. Raman concluded that timing protein intake is key.

Text 2
Few dispute that older adults need ample protein to preserve muscle. But in Raman's trial, the even-split group also ate about 15 grams more protein per day, so the strength gains may reflect quantity rather than timing.
choices: Getting enough protein helps older adults keep their muscle mass.
Spreading protein across meals builds more strength than eating it at dinner.
The strength gains in Raman's trial came from eating more total protein.
Older adults should eat more of their protein at dinner than at other meals.
explanation: The dispute is about timing versus quantity. Both authors start from the same premise. Text 1 opens by saying that older adults lose muscle partly because they eat too little protein, and Text 2 says that 'few dispute that older adults need ample protein to preserve muscle.'

B.why: This is Raman's conclusion. Text 2 challenges it by pointing out that the even-split group also ate more protein.

C.why: You took Text 2's side and made it stronger. Text 2 says the gains 'may' reflect quantity, and Text 1 attributes them to timing.

D.why: Neither author recommends this. Text 1's trial found that the dinner-heavy group gained less strength.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Immune activity rises and falls on a daily cycle. Immunologist Kenji Watanabe vaccinated 300 adults over 60 against influenza either between 9 and 11 a.m. or between 3 and 5 p.m. The morning group produced markedly higher antibody levels a month later, leading Watanabe to urge clinics to schedule all flu shots before noon.

Text 2
Watanabe's morning advantage appears genuine, but it may not extend beyond older people. In a follow-up with adults aged 20 to 40, antibody levels did not differ by appointment time, perhaps because younger immune systems respond strongly at any hour.
choices: Clinics should give all flu shots before noon to make them most effective.
Younger adults' immune systems respond strongly to vaccines at any hour.
Morning flu shots lower older adults' chances of catching influenza.
The time of day a flu shot is given can affect older adults' antibody levels.
explanation: Text 2 limits the scope of Text 1's claim to older people but does not reject it. Text 1 found higher antibody levels in older adults vaccinated in the morning, and Text 2 says that this 'morning advantage appears genuine' for older people. Both texts support the claim for that group.

A.why: This is Watanabe's broad recommendation. Text 2 questions it because younger adults showed no difference by appointment time.

B.why: This is only Text 2's tentative explanation, introduced with 'perhaps.' Text 1 says nothing about younger adults.

C.why: Both texts measure antibody levels, not infection rates. You treated a lab measure as proof of protection against illness, which neither author claims.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Across the Ardel Valley, grasshopper sparrow counts have fallen by 40 percent since 2000, the same period in which farmers began cutting hay three weeks earlier. Ornithologist Lena Fischer found that early mowing destroyed most nests in cut fields. She concludes that mowing dates are the main driver of the decline.

Text 2
Early mowing undeniably wipes out nests, and those losses cost the population. Yet sparrows have declined just as steeply on Ardel reserves where hay is never cut before August, which points to a cause beyond the valley, such as shrinking winter grasslands.
choices: Earlier mowing is the chief reason the valley's sparrows have declined.
Loss of winter grassland explains why the valley's sparrows have declined.
Nests destroyed by early hay mowing contribute to sparrow losses in the valley.
Sparrows nesting on Ardel reserves have declined less than those on farms.
explanation: The authors disagree about the main cause of the decline. Both accept that mowing does some harm. Text 1 reports that early mowing 'destroyed most nests in cut fields,' and Text 2 grants that it 'undeniably wipes out nests' and that 'those losses cost the population.'

A.why: This is Fischer's conclusion. Text 2 disputes it because sparrows declined just as steeply where hay is cut late.

B.why: This is Text 2's suggested alternative, stated more firmly than Text 2 states it. Text 1 never mentions winter habitat.

D.why: Text 2 says that the reserves declined 'just as steeply,' not less. This choice reverses what the passage reports.
